lead.text: *The practical business literacy every professional needs — even those not in business roles.*

Whether or not you work in business, your work exists inside a business. Understanding how businesses actually operate — the customer, the value, the cost, the risk — makes you more effective at every level, from engineering to marketing to operations.
This playbook is the compressed version. Not an MBA. The actual practical shape.

entries.title: The five questions every business answers (or fails)

blocks.text: **THE TOOL — The core interrogation**

1. Who is the customer, specifically?
2. What problem are we solving for them, and how painful is it?
3. Why us? What makes us better positioned than the alternatives?
4. What does it cost us to solve it, and what can they pay?
5. How defensible is our position — what stops someone else from copying us?
Any business that can't answer all five clearly is in trouble, whether or not the numbers currently look good.
**THE IDEA — Value is what someone would pay you to solve**

Businesses succeed to the extent that they identify a real problem, solve it better than alternatives, and capture some fraction of the value they create.
Notice the word REAL. Businesses that solve imaginary problems — even elegantly — do not last. The market will patiently reveal which category you're in.
**THE TOOL — The four questions to actually ask customers**

Not 'do you like our product.' They will say yes to be polite.
1. 'Walk me through the last time you had to solve [problem]. What did you do?'
2. 'What was the most frustrating part of that?'
3. 'How much did that cost you — in time, money, or stress?'
4. 'If [category of solution] didn't exist, how would you solve this today?'
Notice: no leading questions, no product mention, no 'what would you want.' Behavior beats intention. Their actual past behavior is a better predictor than their imagined future behavior.
Most companies have competition. The question is not 'do we have competitors?' It is 'what makes us the obvious choice for our specific customer?'
**THE TOOL — The differentiation test**

Fill in these blanks:
'We are the [category] for [specific customer type] who [want or need X], because [we do Y better than anyone else] — and [Z is the specific proof].'
If any blank is fuzzy, your differentiation is fuzzy. Fuzzy differentiation loses to sharp differentiation over time, even when the sharp competitor is objectively worse.
A business is a machine that converts inputs to outputs. The inputs cost money. The outputs generate money. The difference is what the business gets to keep.
**THE TOOL — The unit economics test**

For any product or service, ask:
• What does it cost us to produce one unit? (COGS)
• What can we charge for one unit? (Price)
• Are we profitable per unit, or losing money on every one and hoping volume fixes it?
• What is our payback period on customer acquisition — how long does it take before a customer has paid us back what we spent to get them?
Businesses that don't have unit economics under control are speculating, not operating. Sometimes the speculation works. More often it does not.

Every business runs on a network of small operational risks: employee turnover, key-person dependencies, customer concentration, regulatory exposure, technology fragility. Most companies fail slowly, not dramatically — small risks compounding until the machine breaks.
**THE TOOL — The five-risk audit**

Once a quarter, list your business's top 5 risks:
1. Customer concentration (any single customer over 20%?).
2. Key person dependencies (does the business collapse if any single person leaves?).
3. Regulatory (any pending changes that could materially affect the business?).
4. Technology / operational (any single system whose failure would halt operations for >24 hours?).
5. Competitive (any credible competitor with clear advantages, or a substitute technology emerging?).
For each, assign a mitigation and an owner. Review quarterly.
Businesses that learn fastest usually win. Learning speed is a function of how many experiments you run, how honest you are about results, and how quickly you incorporate the lessons.
**THE TOOL — The disciplined experiment**

Before running an experiment:
• What is the specific question we're trying to answer?
• What is our current best guess (hypothesis)?
• What would prove us wrong (falsifiable)?
• What is the minimum viable test — the cheapest, fastest thing that would tell us?
• Who decides what we do with the result, and when?
Then run it. Then decide. Do not run experiments whose results you plan to ignore.
**THE GREAT MINDS COUNCIL — On the shape of a business**

Through Peter Drucker's lens:
'The purpose of a business is to create a customer.' Not to maximize shareholder value. Not to grow at all costs. To create — and keep — customers.
Through Jeff Bezos's lens:
'Your margin is my opportunity.' Every fat incumbent is a signal to a leaner competitor.
Through Warren Buffett's lens:
'It's far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than a fair company at a wonderful price.' Business quality compounds; price is temporary.
Through Andy Grove's lens:
'Only the paranoid survive.' The comfortable assumption is usually the one that eventually kills the company.
Through Michael Porter's lens:
Strategy is choosing what NOT to do. Companies that try to be everything to everyone become nothing to anyone.
Through Clayton Christensen's lens:
'What job is the customer hiring your product to do?' If you don't know, you're competing on features rather than value.
Where the Council might be wrong:
Business frameworks are compressions of complex reality. Applied rigidly, they mislead. Applied as questions, they clarify.
REMEMBER THIS
*“A business is a machine that converts value for someone into money for you. Fix the 'value for someone' part first.”*
